name: Asparagus
summary: A long-lived perennial vegetable grown for spring spears. Home gardeners can begin from seed or crowns; seed-grown plants take longer to reach harvest.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Asparagus officinalis. This is the garden crop species with no named cultivar specified; seed-grown plants and planted crowns are distinct establishment routes.

cultivation.short: Choose a permanent, sunny, well-drained bed
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension describes asparagus as a long-lived perennial requiring a carefully selected site, adequate moisture and weed control. Its bed spacing and soil preparation are field-garden guidance, not container or hydroponic instructions.

growth.short: Perennial crowns send up edible spears and fern-like tops
growth.guidance: Kew describes the accepted species as perennial; UMN explains that spears arise from underground crowns and grow into ferns that replenish reserves. Mature plant form is not treated as a small-space crop assumption.

harvest.short: Harvest only after establishment; protect fern growth
harvest.guidance: UMN advises waiting two years after crown planting or three years after seed planting before harvest, then limiting the harvest period so foliage can rebuild crown reserves. This is regional home-garden guidance, not a hydroponic timetable.

problems.short: Weeds and late frost can harm establishment or spears
problems.guidance: UMN notes that young seedlings compete poorly with weeds and that late spring frost can kill emerged spears. No disease resistance or indoor compatibility is claimed.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited sources cover long-lived outdoor bed culture, not recirculating hydroponics.

growthHabits.reason: The controlled vocabulary does not encode asparagus crown and fern architecture.

height.reason: No single cultivar-specific mature dimension is selected for this crop identity.

spread.reason: The cited row/bed spacing is not a mature spread value or indoor spacing recommendation.

spacing.reason: Field bed spacing is not a hydroponic position or pod recommendation.

light.reason: The outdoor sunny-site advice is not translated into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Rhubarb
summary: A large, cold-hardy perennial vegetable harvested for cooked leaf stalks. Seed starting is documented, while divisions are a practical way to establish or share known plants; leaves and roots are not food.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Rheum rhabarbarum in Polygonaceae. This profile is the species-level garden crop, not a red-stalk cultivar; UMN notes that size, color, sourness and fiber vary among varieties.

cultivation.short: Allow substantial space in a well-drained site
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension describes a large perennial plant suited to well-drained garden soil and notes a typical 3-by-3-foot garden area. This is outdoor garden guidance and does not establish container or hydroponic compatibility.

growth.short: Large perennial crown; varieties differ in vigor and stalk traits
growth.guidance: UMN describes rhubarb as a perennial that can live for many years; green-stalked varieties are often more vigorous and longer-stalked than red types. No color or size is assigned to an unspecified cultivar.

harvest.short: Harvest petioles after establishment; discard leaves
harvest.guidance: UMN advises waiting until the second season to harvest established plants, or the third season when started from seed. Only the stalks are edible; leaves are toxic and should be removed and discarded.

maintenance.short: Divide a mature crown when it becomes crowded or unproductive
maintenance.guidance: UMN explains that the crown expands outward and may benefit from division every few years. Division is a practical vegetative route; it does not mean seed propagation is impossible.

problems.short: Do not eat the leaves; drainage and crown health matter
problems.guidance: UMN identifies rhubarb leaves as toxic and notes crown/root rot risk in wet or poorly drained conditions. This is safety and crop-level care guidance, not a diagnosis of an individual plant.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited guidance describes a large outdoor perennial, not hydroponic production.

growthHabits.reason: The controlled vocabulary does not represent a large perennial crown and broad leaf canopy.

height.reason: No species-level numeric mature height is needed or established here.

spread.reason: Garden bed area is not a plant spread measurement or indoor spacing.

spacing.reason: The recommended garden area is not converted to a hydroponic position.

light.reason: All-day outdoor sun advice is not mapped to an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Escarole
summary: A broad-leaved form of endive grown as a salad and cooking green. It shares crop-level culture with other chicories, while its broad, smoother leaves distinguish it from curly endive.

identity.short: Accepted species: Cichorium endivia; broad-leaved escarole type
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Cichorium endivia. UMN Extension distinguishes escarole as a broad, smooth-leaved form of endive and curly endive as another type; this record does not name a cultivar.

cultivation.short: Cool-season chicory culture; keep shallow roots moist
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension groups escarole with chicories and gives regional seed-starting, direct-seeding and soil-moisture guidance for the crop group. Minnesota planting dates and field spacing are not generalized to other climates or indoor pods.

growth.short: Broad, smooth leaves distinguish escarole from curly endive
growth.guidance: The Extension source explicitly describes escarole as a form of endive with broader, smoother leaves. That is a horticultural type distinction within Cichorium endivia, not a separate species or named cultivar.

harvest.short: Use leaves as a salad or cooking green
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension describes escarole as a salad and cooking green and recommends frequent leaf harvest for fresh salads across the guide's leafy crop scope. No cultivar-specific harvest date is assigned.

problems.short: Heat, dry soil and bolting can reduce quality
problems.guidance: UMN reports that the chicory group performs best in cool conditions and that heat/long days may cause bolting and bitterness. These are regional crop-level concerns, not cultivar-specific resistance claims.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited source concerns soil-grown chicory crops and does not validate this type in recirculating hydroponics.

growthHabits.reason: A controlled compatibility habit class is not established for this crop type.

height.reason: No specific mature height is selected for the broad-leaved type.

spread.reason: The crop guide's spacing is not a mature spread measurement.

spacing.reason: Field spacing varies with harvest stage and is not converted to indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor cool-season guidance is not mapped to a grow-light tier.
